headline: Recommended data center zoning ordinance to full Council after removing 2-megawatt threshold and adding accessory server exemption, 5-0.
summary: Members discussed a proposed data center zoning ordinance, including a 2-megawatt threshold and an exemption for servers that support another lawful use on the same premises. Members voted 5-0 to strike the 2-megawatt language and 5-0 to add the accessory-use exemption. They then voted 5-0 to send the amended ordinance to the full Council with a positive recommendation.
decisions: Approved striking the 2 megawatts aggregate language from the data center ordinance, 5-0.
Approved amending the data center ordinance to exclude accessory server equipment used with another lawful principal use, 5-0.
Recommended the amended data center ordinance to the full Council, 5-0.

Roll call vote – 5-0 motion carries.

plain_text:
City of Salem, Massachusetts 
 
“Know Your Rights Under the Open Meeting Law, M.G.L. c. 30A ss. 18-25 and  
City Ordinance Sections 2-2028 through 2-2033.” 
 
The City Council Committee on     Ordinances, Licenses and Legal Affairs co-posted Committee of the 
Whole______________________________________________________________________________  
met in the Council Chamber on _September 30, 2026__________ at ______6:00______P.M. 
for the purpose of discussing the matters(s) listed below.  Notice of this meeting was posted on  
___ September 28, 2026__ at ___        9:56 A.M._________________ 
(This meeting is being recorded) 
ATTENDANCE 
OLLA – Varela (chair), Holappa, Prosniewski, Hapworth and Smith (zoom) COW – Merkl, Sydoriak, Turowski, Davis, King.  Also, 
in attendance Planning Board member Josh Turiel and Robin Stein, KP Law.    
ABSENT WERE:  COW - Flynn 
Ordinance to Amend Ordinance relative to Zoning – Data Centers 
Varela explained that the data center ordinance had passed first passage the previous Thursday and was now before 
committee ahead of second passage, with the Planning Board recommending an amendment adding an aggregate power 
threshold of 2 megawatts to the definition of a data center. He cautioned that because the original proposal was an outright 
ban, the Council needed to stay within the “four corners” of the existing ordinance when considering changes. Although the 
Planning Board had discussed options such as special permits and more specific data center classifications, he said those 
broader changes could fall outside the scope of the current proposal and would likely need to be addressed in a future 
discussion. 
Hapworth asked for Turiel to speak regarding planning board’s recommendation.   
Turiel explained that the Planning Board initially faced a problem because the proposed data center ordinance was written as 
an outright ban without definitions, potentially prohibiting ordinary data-processing uses such as server rooms in corporate 
offices. The board therefore sought to create a definition that would allow routine data-processing equipment while 
preventing large, resource-intensive hyperscale data centers. He said the proposed 2-megawatt threshold, which is used in 
other communities including Mansfield, was intended as a short-term solution.  He said the ordinance should ultimately be 
rewritten to establish different tiers of data centers, with varying permitting standards for uses that could be allowed by right, 
require a special permit, or be prohibited entirely. He characterized the current proposal as a temporary measure to address 
the issue while the city develops a more comprehensive “version 2.0.” The goal, he said, is to keep routine data-processing 
uses legal while preventing very large hyperscale facilities that would be unusually large by Salem standards. 
Hapworth questioned whether a megawatt threshold is the best way to define a data center, suggesting that the ordinance 
instead should explicitly define server rooms as incidental uses to a primary business. He expressed concern that a 2-megawatt 
threshold could create ambiguity for facilities just below the megawatt limit.
Turiel explained that the Planning Board had discussed this approach, but the board and city solicitors concluded they were 
constrained by the original wording of the ordinance and had to remain within the “four corners” of what had been publicly 
noticed and presented at the joint public hearing.  Adding language specifically exempting server rooms or requiring them to 
be incidental to another primary use was viewed as going beyond the scope of the original ordinance and would therefore 
need to be addressed through a separate process. 
Stein said the ordinance’s existing language appears intended to regulate data centers as a principal or primary use, meaning 
the Council could likely add clarifying language stating that ordinary server equipment used as an accessory to another primary 
use would not be considered a data center, while remaining within the scope of the original proposal. She cautioned that 
relying solely on a megawatt threshold could create gaps for facilities that fall below the threshold and recommended 
revisiting the ordinance more comprehensively. She said the Council could instead clarify that businesses such as banks with 
servers would not be treated as data centers when the equipment is accessory to the business’s primary use and does not 
serve third parties; in her view, that would clarify rather than change the original intent and could reasonably remain within 
the ordinance’s existing scope. 
Holappa said the concern extends beyond hyperscale data centers to high-heat and high-noise facilities that could be located 
in industrial zones near residential neighborhoods, particularly if facilities under the 2-megawatt threshold could be allowed 
close to homes. She clarified that the recent Shetland Park proposal was denied because data centers are currently not a 
permitted use under Salem’s zoning, rather than because of its size, and argued that leaving the current prohibition in place 
would be preferable to adopting a flawed ordinance. She also said the city should consider how data centers interact with 
existing principal and accessory uses, such as hospitals with server rooms, as well as existing zoning categories for 
telecommunications, essential services, and research facilities. Overall, she urged the Council to start over and develop a 
comprehensive ordinance that addresses the different uses and residents’ concerns about locating data centers near 
neighborhoods. 
Varela clarified that existing server rooms, such as those in hospitals, would be considered nonconforming uses if the 
ordinance passed and therefore could continue operating, although future expansions requiring new permits could be 
affected. 
Stein said clarifying “primary use” would make clear that the ordinance targets businesses whose primary purpose is server 
storage or data processing, rather than existing businesses that use servers to support their main operations. She also noted 
that the ZBA decision regarding the recent data center in Shetland Park could still be appealed in court, creating uncertainty 
about how a court might rule, and said the Council could use the ordinance to address that uncertainty.   
Holappa asked if Stein has a recommendation on how we can add the principal use language?  She asked how the ordinance 
could more clearly distinguish data centers as a principal use from server rooms that support another business, noting that 
data centers appear in the industrial principal-use table and the definition refers to facilities “primarily designed or used” for 
data center activities.  
Stein said we could work with the language a bit to make clear that if the primary purpose is a data center, then it is not 
allowed.  She said the ordinance could be clarified by adding language to the definition of a data center, potentially using 
“principal” instead of “primary,” to distinguish facilities whose main purpose is data storage or processing from server rooms 
and technology equipment that support another lawful use on the same premises. She emphasized that the wording should 
clearly refer to the specific business or unit rather than an entire property with multiple uses, explaining that facilities primarily 
devoted to data center operations would be regulated as data centers, while equipment serving another principal use would 
be excluded. 
Holappa asked what does the path forward look like for the organization that lost the appeal with the ZBA? 
Stein explained that once the ZBA decision is filed with the City Clerk, there is a period during which it can be appealed to 
court, where a judge would interpret the zoning bylaw and either uphold or reject the ZBA and city’s position. In response to a 
question about the city’s role if an appeal were filed, the discussion indicated that the city would need to participate in 
defending the final decision, with further details potentially handled in executive session.  The city would have the right to 
defend its decision.
Holappa asked whether use-based zoning restrictions have a long history of legal precedent, including Supreme Court 
litigation, and whether clearly defining prohibited uses would make the ordinance more legally defensible against challenges 
from well-funded data center companies. 
Stein explained that Massachusetts communities have authority under the Zoning Act to determine which uses are permitted, 
regulated, or prohibited, and noted that the Attorney General’s approval of Mansfield’s data center bylaw provides a useful 
starting point, although court challenges could lead to a different outcome. She said data centers are a relatively new land use, 
and, as with short-term rentals, clearer legal guidance will likely emerge over time as courts consider challenges to local 
regulations. 
Holappa asked whether there are measures residents can pursue to mitigate the impacts of a data center, such as noise or 
other disturbances, after it has already been permitted and established in an industrial zone surrounded by residential 
neighborhoods. 
Stein suggested that Salem could eventually consider a data center overlay district, using planning analysis to identify specific 
areas where data centers of varying sizes could be permitted based on neighborhood compatibility and available 
infrastructure, rather than allowing them throughout all industrial districts. 
Holappa said they need to be intentional on whatever they pass, because if data center goes in, it is impossible to get rid of it 
and the residents will suffer.  
King asked whether, if the Council took no action on the proposed ordinance, the city’s current position that data centers are 
not a permitted use under Salem’s zoning would be legally vulnerable to challenge. 
Stein said the city’s position that data centers are not currently a permitted use is not necessarily legally shaky, but it could be 
disputed in court, creating some legal uncertainty. She added that clarifying the ordinance to exclude technology equipment 
that is accessory to another principal use would likely fall within the scope of the existing proposal because it would clarify the 
definition rather than change its intent. 
King asked whether clarifying the accessory-use exemption would be a permissible amendment within the scope of the current 
ordinance, rather than requiring a new proposal.  She expressed concern that a business could exploit the accessory-use 
exemption by claiming its technology business was not the principal use despite housing substantial server equipment, and 
asked Stein to confirm whether the Planning Board’s proposed 2-megawatt limit would fall outside the scope of the current 
ordinance. 
Stein said the proposed 2-megawatt threshold was not necessarily outside the ordinance’s scope, but could create ambiguity 
elsewhere in the ordinance, whereas changing prohibited uses to allow special-permit approval would more clearly exceed the 
scope of the original ban. 
King asked if it was the same ambiguity that we already have with it not being addressed in the current ordinance. 
Stein said it is a different ambiguity.  We are simply trying to stop any kind of data centers that are the primary and not 
accessory uses.   
King said that passing this as is has some benefits and some risks.  It sounds like Hapworth has some language that will address 
the accessory use that may be a reasonable way to get this on the books at least short term.   
Hapworth explained, so we understand what language we're talking about, in this ordinance it says, for purposes of this 
ordinance, a data center shall not be considered an office, warehouse, manufacturing, or research use.  And then I would add 
after that, a data center shall not include server rooms or related equipment that primarily support and are incidental and 
subordinate to another lawful principal use on the same premises. This exception does not cover a separate business 
providing data storage, server hosting, or computing services to third parties.   Hopefully that addresses the concerns and 
questions we have about not wanting to inadvertently outlaw something that is reasonable, but also not wanting to open the 
door on 1.9 megawatts and lower, and what that may entail.
Turiel explained that current-generation AI servers can require about 4,000 watts each, compared with roughly 1,000 to 1,500 
watts for more routine servers used for web hosting and similar purposes. He said AI workloads often require hundreds or 
thousands of servers in a single facility, along with substantial power and cooling infrastructure, which helps explain why large 
AI data centers are generally located in areas with significant power and water resources and away from densely populated 
areas. Turiel also noted that there are many levels of data-processing facilities, from server rooms and hosting facilities to 
large data centers and gave examples of existing Salem facilities that contain significant server and backup-power 
infrastructure without resembling large hyperscale facilities.  He said language distinguishing a principal use from an accessory 
or incidental use would make sense because businesses can have substantial server equipment without operating a data 
center as their primary function. He said existing data-processing operations in Salem would likely remain permissible under 
either the proposed language or the 2-megawatt threshold. However, he recommended that the city eventually return with a 
more nuanced ordinance establishing clearer distinctions among different types and scales of data centers, potentially using 
Mansfield's recently adopted approach as a model. 
Holappa said she likes Hapworth’s added language with the original language but without the 2-megawatt amendment.  She is 
more comfortable passing the ordinance with the added clarification. 
King said she hates having to change an ordinance only to fix it later.  She is in favor of the additional language as a short fix but 
thinks they should work urgently to put a new ordinance in place. 
Smith had a question for Turiel.  What would be an example of a use case for under 2 megawatts that fits the definition of a 
data center?  And what would be the beneficial use be to the community or businesses nearby? 
Turiel said a scaled down version of the use that was just turned down by the ZBA would fit in the definition.  He said you can 
use the hospital as an example of an accessory use.  If they were going to add more space to add servers, they might have 
trouble getting it.  It isn’t likely that another issue comes up while we work to get an ordinance in place that is more 
permanent.  Whatever the outcome is, he said they should look at ordinances from other cities and towns and get this right.  
He said they are in this because this is the language that was given to them.  He said Hapworth’s language is an excellent way 
to clarify accessory use.  
Smith asked if the hospital use case that Turiel stated would be a ZBA hardship. 
Stein said the ordinance was intended to regulate facilities primarily used for data storage or server hosting, not existing lawful 
businesses such as hospitals or banks that maintain servers for their own operations. She supported adding clarifying language 
to explicitly exempt accessory technology uses, explaining that this would reflect the ordinance’s original intent and prevent 
future disputes over its interpretation. 
Smith supported Hepworth’s language clarifying the exemption for accessory technology uses but argued that Salem should 
ban data centers at any power capacity until the Council fully understands their potential noise, energy, heat, and water 
impacts. He emphasized that the ordinance could be amended later if a specific proposal demonstrated a need for an 
exception. 
Stein clarified that Salem’s zoning ordinance does not allow the Zoning Board of Appeals to grant commercial-use variances, so 
an applicant challenging the city’s interpretation could file an administrative appeal or ask the City Council to amend the 
ordinance. 
Sydoriak supported Hapworth’s amendments.  He said they clarified and strengthened the ordinance and urged the Council to 
establish a committee promptly to develop a more carefully crafted, comprehensive data center policy. He emphasized the 
need to support local small businesses’ technology needs while preventing large data center corporations from entering the 
city without adequate safeguards. 
Merkl thanked Stein and Turiel for the informative discussion, expressed concern that a 2-megawatt exemption could create 
ambiguity and leave the ordinance vulnerable to challenges from well-funded companies, and supported clarifying the ban 
while acknowledging both concerns about rushing the process and the need to act promptly.
Turowski said she was a little tentative about the revisions, but she feels better about it now that Turiel has said that the 
language that Hapworth has proposed is ok.  She said she wouldn’t want to include the 2 megawatts because that opens a 
door for a company to work around the ordinance.    
Turiel recommended retaining the 2-megawatt threshold while also adding Hapworth’s language exempting servers accessory 
to other lawful uses, providing a dual safeguard. He said the proposed Shetland Park facility required 6 megawatts, while a 2-
megawatt limit could accommodate many legitimate smaller server facilities without allowing the large-scale operations that 
place greater demands on electricity, cooling, water, and infrastructure. Citing facilities at Cummings Center as examples, he 
argued that data centers are not inherently problematic; the main concern is large-scale operations that Salem may lack the 
resources to support. He emphasized that the current proposal is an interim measure constrained by how it was originally filed, 
and that the Council should develop a more comprehensive ordinance establishing tiers for uses allowed by right, requiring 
special permits, or prohibited altogether. 
Stein said the proposed language would clarify that a data center does not include computer servers and related information-
technology infrastructure that are accessory, incidental, or subordinate to another lawful principal use of the same facility. It 
would also specify that the exception does not apply to a separate business providing data storage, server hosting, or similar 
technology services, with a suggestion to remove the broader term “computing services” because it could unintentionally 
encompass ordinary IT businesses. 
 
Public Comment –  
Steve Kapantis argued that the Council should not rush to adopt permanent zoning regulations while acknowledging that the 
current proposal is incomplete, suggesting instead that it consider a six-month moratorium on data centers while developing a 
comprehensive ordinance. He said councillors could take procedural steps to introduce and consider a moratorium rather than 
concluding that they had no options. He also urged the Council to avoid hyperbole and focus on specific impacts that zoning 
can regulate, including noise, power consumption, heat, and water use. He questioned whether a 2-megawatt aggregate-
power limit would effectively regulate facilities that could generate their own electricity and noted that heat and power could 
potentially be recovered or reused for community purposes. He argued that regulating these impacts directly could address 
data centers as well as other industrial facilities with similar resource demands, rather than banning data centers as a category. 
Back to discussion - 
Holappa motioned to strike the language 2 megawatts aggregate and seconded by Hapworth.  Holappa raised concerns that a 
2-megawatt power threshold would not adequately account for a facility’s total heat output, particularly if it relied on diesel 
generators, which produce substantial additional waste heat due to their inefficiency. Drawing on her mechanical engineering 
and industrial experience, she argued that the proposed language did not sufficiently address environmental impacts and that 
these issues should be examined through a more comprehensive future discussion rather than the current ordinance. 
Roll call vote – 5-0 motion carries. 
Hapworth motioned to amend language after a data center shall not be considered an office, warehouse, manufacturing, or 
research use.  He said to add the language, a data center shall not include such computer servers and related information 
technology infrastructure that is accessory, incidental, and subordinate to a lawful principal use at the same facility. or portion 
thereof, however stored. This exception does not cover a separate business providing data storage, server hosting, or similar 
technology to third parties. The motion was seconded by Holappa.   
Stein confirmed that was the appropriate language to not allow data centers as a principal use.   
Turiel said he would suggest they add distributing and processing or similar to the use definition if you are removing the 2 
megawatts aggregate.  Distributed processing is something that would cover a CPU rental base for large-scale distributed work 
over multiple processors, multiple servers. That covers AI usage and a lot of other usage. Without that addition, someone 
could come in to have a use for hire, renting for storage, etc.
Holappa noted that eventually a zoning officer will have to interpret it, so we want to be mindful of that when we are adding 
technical language.   
Hapworth clarified the language they were adding stating for purposes of this ordinance, a data center shall not be considered 
an office, warehouse, manufacturing, or research use and said they should add the language, a data center shall not include 
such computer servers, and related information technology infrastructure. It is accessory, incidental, and subordinate to a 
lawful principal use at the same facility, or portion thereof, however stored. This exception does not cover a separate business 
providing data storage, server hosting, and adding in distributed processing or similar technology to third parties. 
Roll call vote – 5-0. 
Hapworth moved to send this to full council with positive recommendation and seconded by Holappa. 
Roll call vote 5-0. 
On the motion of C. Hapworth, the meeting adjourned at 7:23P.M. 
 
        
       Andrew Varela                                          mbc 
           (Chairperson)
